paras: The lynching of Frank Fisher took place on the afternoon of Sunday, April 30, 1882, at Galion, Crawford County, Ohio, when a crowd took Fisher, a Black man, from the city prison and hanged him in nearby woods. Fisher had been accused of raping a 13-year-old German girl two days earlier, and he protested his innocence to the end. Papers across the country carried the story, several remarking that the lynchers were unmasked and acted in daylight on a Sunday in Ohio.

According to a correspondent at Galion, Fisher had been chopping wood near the home of Barbara Rettig and was accused of assaulting her in the woods there at noon on Friday, April 28, after which he left town. A dispatch dated April 29 reported several hundred men hunting the accused, there called "Jerry Myers," and stated that "if found he will be lynched"; a local Ohio item called him "Frank Smith" and reported a $100 reward from the mayor.

Galion officers T. J. Wurts and W. H. W. Nichols arrested Fisher about 5 a.m. on April 30 at Fredericktown, Knox County, as he was leaving on foot; he at first denied his name. He reached Galion about 11:30 a.m. and was locked in an iron cage in the City Hall prison while the mayor and city officers planned to move him to the county jail at Bucyrus or another county.

At 3 p.m. an unmasked crowd carrying hammers, crowbars and a rope demanded the prisoner. The officers refused, and Mayor Underwood, G. M. Zeigler and others urged the crowd to let the law take its course, but the crowd forced the doors, broke open the cage and dragged Fisher into the street. The Cincinnati Commercial's special added that locomotive whistles and fire bells sounded and that "negroes joined in the mob and a negro broke open the cell."

After a delegation with a physician confirmed that the girl could identify him, the crowd marched Fisher to the Rettig house at the foot of South Market Street, where she reportedly said "That is the man" and fainted. The crowd first dragged him to a tree behind the house, then took him to the woods described as the scene of the alleged assault. Allowed a short prayer, Fisher said, "O Lord, take care of me. I know that I am going to die, but I have many friends," before his hands were tied, his face covered and he was hanged at 4:10 p.m. The correspondent wrote that at least 2,000 men, women and children, many from Bucyrus, Mt. Gilead and Crestline, watched, and that the body still hung at 9 p.m.

The correspondent reported that the county coroner had been notified and might hold an inquest that night, and that there was "some talk" of having the leading lynchers indicted, though it "would not be safe to attempt that at present." No inquest verdict, arrest of lynchers or indictment appears in the coverage. Local opinion was described differently: the Cincinnati Commercial said many in Galion condemned the lynching, while the correspondent wrote that Fisher had no sympathy from anyone who knew the particulars.

The news first reached the national press through a Cleveland dispatch giving a mob of about 200 men, which ran as a single line in papers from Wheeling to Helena and Cheyenne. Fuller accounts came from the Cincinnati Commercial's special and from a correspondent's report credited to the Cleveland Herald, which Ohio weeklies at Napoleon, Perrysburg and Hillsboro reprinted.

White papers treated the accusation as fact, calling Fisher a "negro ravisher," a "black beast" and, in the Wheeling Intelligencer's headline, "A Black Fiend." The St. Paul Globe headed its story "The Minneapolis Plan," linking it to the lynching of Frank McManus at Minneapolis two days before, and later round-ups grouped the two cases under "Judge Lynch." The Eaton Democrat said the lynching met "universal approval," whereas the Somerset Press, while stating Fisher's guilt, called a daylight Sunday lynching by an unmasked mob in Ohio "unusual."

Crowd estimates differ widely: about 200 in the Cleveland dispatch, about 300 in the Indiana State Sentinel, 2,000 at the jail and 4,000 at the hanging in the Cincinnati Commercial, and at least 2,000 in the correspondent's report.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Fisher
bases: A crowd forced the Galion City Hall prison, took Frank Fisher from officers and hanged him in the woods (A6, A8, A23).

Fisher was taken from the city prison over the refusal of officers and the mayor's appeals and hanged by a crowd numbered from about 200 to several thousand (A6, A8, A23); the crowd acted on the accusation that he had raped a 13-year-old girl, saying a lawful trial would only send him to the penitentiary (A23).

A Cleveland wire report (A8, A12), a Cincinnati Commercial special (A8) and a Cleveland Herald correspondent on the scene (A14, A23) independently agree on the jail break, the identification and the hanging.

accounts.label: Cleveland wire report
accounts.gist: Fisher, said to have ravished a 13-year-old girl, was lynched at Galion at 4 p.m. by about 200 (or 300) men; he made no resistance and choked to death.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial special
accounts.gist: Over 2,000 people broke open the jail, with Black residents joining and one breaking the cell; after the girl's identification a crowd of 4,000 hanged him at the scene; many in Galion condemned it.

accounts.label: Cleveland Herald correspondent at Galion
accounts.gist: Detailed narrative of the arrest, the forcing of the City Hall prison against the mayor's appeals, the identification, Fisher's prayer and protest of innocence, and the hanging in the woods before at least 2,000 spectators.

framing.detail: The on-the-scene correspondent called Fisher 'the negro rapist' and a 'black beast', presented the bloodstains and the girl's identification as proof, and wrote that he had no sympathy from anyone, while calling the affair 'to be regretted'.
The Eaton Democrat said the 'decision of Judge Lynch' met 'universal approval' and that such men 'should be strung up without waiting on the law'.
The St. Paul Globe headlined it 'The Minneapolis Plan' and described Fisher as hanged 'by Indignant Citizens'; the Wheeling Intelligencer headed it 'A Black Fiend Lynched'.
Most distant papers ran one-line wire briefs naming Fisher as 'colored' or a 'negro ravisher', often beside the Minneapolis lynching of the same week.
The Somerset Press stated his guilt but remarked that a lynching 'in Ohio, by an unmasked mob, in broad daylight, and on Sunday—was unusual'.
